extracted.intended_audience: federal and state agency officials, administrative law practitioners, policymakers, regulators, and legal scholars interested in notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and policy guidance for how agencies should detect, treat, and evaluate mass, computer-generated, and malattributed public comments in notice-and-comment rulemaking. Covers technical de-duplication practices, criminal-law theories, APA obligations, and policy tradeoffs for accepting, ignoring, or removing problematic comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: De-duplication thresholds for mass comment campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies need to set the policies by which they decide how much overlap must exist between comments before they qualify as being part of a mass comment campaign (and therefore do not review them). De-duplication programs let an agency set the level of overlap (e.g., 90%), and different agencies use different thresholds, though none appears to require 100% overlap for something to qualify as being part of a mass comment campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should select and publish a threshold for overlap (example: 90%); thresholds vary across agencies and do not require 100% identicality. Use of automated de-duplication is common practice but policies must be set by the agency to define what level of similarity triggers batch treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of unique information within batched comments
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent that a participant in a mass comment campaign adds unique information (e.g., submits the organizer’s form comment but then adds a sentence saying “I am personally supportive of this rule because . . . .”), agencies generally review the unique information, even if the identical content is batched and treated as a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when comments are grouped as duplicates, agencies should inspect and consider any added unique substantive material rather than discarding the entire submission as part of a mass campaign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posting representative examples for mass comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Some agencies do not post all iterations of comments received on Regulations.gov if they qualify as being part of a mass comment campaign. For instance, certain agencies just post a representative example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may choose to publicly post a representative comment instead of every near-identical iteration; this practice affects transparency and public review of the full record and should be governed by clear agency policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Malattributed comments differ from mass and computer-generated comments in two critical ways: First, malattributed comments involve a direct falsehood; the submitter makes an assertion about its identity that is untrue. Second, they may cause harm not just to the notice-and-comment process, but to some individuals outside that process, namely, those whose names have been used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize malattributed comments as involving an explicit false claim about authorship/identity and potentially implicating harms to third parties (e.g., identity theft).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry whether malattributed comments constitute criminal activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether this activity constitutes a crime is central to the appropriate agency response for three reasons: (1) if it is criminal, prosecution/referral to DOJ is an option; (2) criminality increases the agency's obligation to discourage/prevent it; (3) criminal designation signals societal seriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and policymakers should evaluate criminal-law theories carefully because the availability (or not) of criminal remedies shapes enforcement and policy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud elements applied to malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard definition of fraud has five elements: (1) a false statement of a material fact, (2) knowledge on the part of the defendant that the statement is untrue, (3) intent on the part of the defendant to deceive the alleged victim, (4) justifiable reliance by the alleged victim on the statement, and (5) injury to the alleged victim as a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malattributed comments satisfy some elements (a false statement) but often fail others in the rulemaking context—especially reliance and injury—because agencies typically do not rely on commenter identities and tangible injury to agency property is hard to show. Materiality is also problematic if identity does not affect the weight given to a comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited applicability of wire and mail fraud statutes to comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire and mail fraud statutes require that the perpetrator be attempting to obtain 'money or property' from the defrauded party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because influencing policymaking generally does not seek to obtain money or property from the agency, typical malattributed or mass comment campaigns are unlikely to be actionable under ordinary wire/mail fraud statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible applicability of conspiracy to defraud the United States (§ 371)
rubrics_metrics.description: 18 U.S.C. § 371 (conspiracy to defraud the United States) criminalizes conspiracies 'to defraud the United States, or any agency thereof in any manner or for any purpose' and has been read to extend to 'any conspiracy for the purpose of impairing, obstructing, or defeating the lawful function of any department of Government.' Using false identities could be such a deceit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theory can reach mass or malattributed comment campaigns intended to impair agency functions (e.g., to create false impressions of public support or to slow down the agency). However, prosecutions under § 371 are uncommon, proving substantial harm is difficult, and the charge is conspiracy (with its own elements), so prosecutors may be reluctant to proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of the false statements statute (18 U.S.C. § 1001) and materiality
rubrics_metrics.description: 18 U.S.C. § 1001 prohibits knowingly or willfully making 'false, fictitious, or fraudulent' statements 'in any matter within the jurisdiction' of the executive branch. The statute does not require showing financial loss, but the false statement must be material—i.e., 'has a natural tendency to influence, or [is] capable of influencing, the decision of the decisionmaking body.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A false name by itself is immaterial unless the identity influences the weight of the submission. Bespoke malattributed comments that assert relevant expertise or experience (or use a name that communicates such background) could be material and thus potentially actionable under § 1001.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA obligation to accept and consider comments (including potential reach to malattributed comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA requires agencies not just to accept but also to consider comments. Courts have required agencies to respond to all significant comments. Under one reading, these obligations could extend to malattributed comments just like any other comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agency has no clear policy prohibiting malattributed submissions, it is more plausible that the APA would require it to accept and consider such submissions; however, agencies frequently conclude many comments do not require response and malattribution can be a factor supporting that conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency authority to impose reasonable form and content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are unquestionably free to impose reasonable requirements on the form and content of public comments (e.g., comment deadlines). Agencies can ignore late-filed comments and many can prohibit anonymous comments; ACUS recommends agencies establish clear public policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should (and can) adopt and publish clear policies governing anonymous comments, deadlines, civility, and other submission requirements and enforce them consistently; such rules affect the permissibility and weight of malattributed or anonymous comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: No per se APA-based obligation to 'cleanse' the docket of malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: If a comment makes no contribution, the agency does not reject it, it just ignores it. Removing useless comments would require effort and would hinder public participation; thus courts have not required agencies to purge irrelevant comments. For an APA-based purge obligation to follow, the mere presence of malattributed comments must cause affirmative harm, which is hard to identify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should be cautious before undertaking docket purges; absent demonstrable affirmative harm (e.g., confusion caused by a 'deep fake' authoritative submission), ignoring irrelevant or duplicative malattributed comments may be legally defensible and administratively preferable to wholesale removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoned-decisionmaking constraint on agency reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: It would not be reasoned decisionmaking to rely on malattributed comments as a measure of public sentiment or to rely on a comment that purported to be from an authority in a relevant field when it was not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must take care not to treat malattributed submissions as evidence of public support or authoritative expertise. Conversely, if a malattributed submission contains relevant, accurate factual information, an agency may lawfully use that substantive content so long as its reliance is reasonable and explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two distinct misleading harms from malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Malattributed comments can mislead in two ways: (a) misleading the agency about the identity of the commenter and (b) misleading the agency as to public opinion by making it appear more commenters hold a particular view than is the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally agencies will not notice or be misled by commenter names amid large numbers of similar submissions (so (a) is often not a practical concern), but (b) is the more salient policy worry—whether mass or fake comments distort perceptions of public sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightened risk posed by bespoke 'deep fake' malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: A bespoke, sophisticated comment that purports to come from a legitimate authority (e.g., General Counsel of an industry player) could sow confusion at the agency and among other commenters and prompt a perceived need among stakeholders to respond. Because of the impact on other commenters, this is the situation where the argument that the APA requires the agency to remove the comment—assuming it is aware of the malattribution—seems strongest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should prioritize identification and remediation (investigation, possible removal, or clear annotation) of high-risk, targeted malattributed submissions that could materially affect decisionmaking or induce additional stakeholder action.
